title: How to request a recommendation letter from me
summary: What I need from you, and what to attach, so I can write a strong and accurate recommendation letter quickly.
body:
Thank you for thinking of me. Before you ask, please commit to following all the guidelines and requirements of your program. Your participation reflects on your institution and on me.

The more complete your answers to the questions below, the faster I can write your letter and the more accurate and specific it will be.

## What I need from you

1. **About you.** Your name, year of study and major.
2. **What you are applying for.** The scholarship, internship, graduate program or other opportunity, and the earliest deadline. If you are applying to several programs, send me a list with each deadline, link and set of instructions for submitting recommendations. Most programs email me a submission link automatically, but some expect me to email someone by the deadline.
3. **How we know each other.** How long I have known you, and in what capacity (instructor, advisor and so on).
4. **Your classes with me.** Which courses you took with me, the grades you earned, and how you stood out.
5. **Projects we worked on.** If we worked together on a project, for example in a data science course, an internship or a research project, describe it and your contributions. Include links to, or copies of, the final work.
6. **What I should emphasize.** What you hope I will speak to: mathematical ability, intellectual curiosity, work ethic, working independently, collaboration, a specific project, or something else.
7. **Why you are a strong candidate.** What makes you particularly qualified for this position, honor or award.
8. **Where you are headed.** Your long-term goals and, if relevant, how this opportunity fits into them.

## Helpful, but optional

9. Four adjectives that describe you well.
10. Your academic accomplishments.
11. Your accomplishments outside of academics, if any.
12. Anything else you would like me to know, such as REUs, summer research, interesting jobs or hobbies.

## What to attach

PDFs are preferred.

- **An unofficial transcript** that is up to date. Most universities let you generate one from the student information system.
- **Your personal statement**, if you have one. Send the latest draft; I am happy to give feedback.
- **Your résumé or CV**, in its latest version.
- **Any other forms** the application requires.

title: CV of failures
summary: The rejections behind the accepted papers and funded grants: my rejected proposals, positions and papers. Placeholder content for now.
body:
> **Placeholder.** My own list is still being compiled. Everything under "Placeholder content" below is the #ShadowCV of Veronika Cheplygina (July 2016), kept here only to show the structure. It will be replaced with my own rejections. Her original post: [My CV of failures](http://www.veronikach.com/thoughts/my-cv-of-failures).

Most CVs list only what went well. Behind every accepted paper, funded grant and job offer there are several rejections, and students rarely see them. This page is my attempt to correct that picture.

title: Useful links
summary: Resources for computer science students and for learning in general: guides, visualizations, interview preparation, project ideas and more.
body:
A collection of resources I recommend to students, for computer science and for learning in general.

## Computer Science

- Matt Might [provides](http://matt.might.net/articles/what-cs-majors-should-know/) a pretty comprehensive guide to what CS students should know. There is not really enough time to get to everything in class, so you will need to put in time outside of class if you want to know all of this. It is worth it, though.
- A nice [collection](https://github.com/nushackers/notes-to-cs-freshmen-from-the-future/blob/master/README.md) of advice and info. Although it says freshman, it will likely be useful to all CS students.
- [Visualizations](https://visualgo.net/) of many algorithms and data structures.
- A [massive list](https://github.com/sdmg15/Best-websites-a-programmer-should-visit) of links for programmers, ranging from tech news to interview preparation to improving your English.
- [Teach Yourself CS](https://teachyourselfcs.com/) is another list of resources. It is aimed toward self-taught software engineers, but the materials could be very useful if you are struggling in a particular course.
- Get better at using the shell with [CMD Challenge](https://cmdchallenge.com/).
- Visualize the code you write using [Python Tutor](http://pythontutor.com/). Despite the name, you can program in Python, Java, JavaScript, C++, and more.
- A collection of [resources](https://github.com/charlax/professional-programming) for programmers.
- Programming interviews are notoriously difficult. There is little evidence to suggest they lead to good hiring decisions, yet I do not think they will change anytime soon. In the meantime, get some practice with the [Tech Interview Handbook](https://yangshun.github.io/tech-interview-handbook/). It gets easier with practice.
- [Here](https://github.com/videogamepreservation) is a fun collection of video game source code from real, commercial games.
- [100+ Project Ideas](https://dev.to/mibzman/100-project-ideas-oda) for programmers or those learning to program.
- [The Interview Study Guide for Software Engineers](https://dev.to/seattledataguy/the-interview-study-guide-for-software-engineers-764).
- [Free-for.dev](https://free-for.dev/): a list of free software and services for developers.
- [Working Well with Legacy Code](http://www.cloudbees.com/blog/working-well-with-legacy-code): software engineering often requires working with an existing code base. This short article is a good description of the mindset you will need to approach such a task. This is becoming even more prevalent due to AI: you will increasingly be asked to fix AI-generated "slop" that worked at first, but quickly became a mess of spaghetti code.

## General Learning

- Coursera's free [Learning How to Learn](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) course will improve your learning of all topics, not just computer science.
- In a similar vein, improving your problem-solving skills will help many facets of your life. This [tutorial](https://ryanstutorials.net/problem-solving-skills/) is a pretty good one. Also check out Polya's [How to Solve It](https://www.amazon.com/How-Solve-Mathematical-Princeton-Science/dp/069116407X).
- I heard you like lists, so [here](https://github.com/jnv/lists) is a list of cool lists.
